headline: F-22 Raptor pilot directs 'wingman' drone in simulated combat
summary: The U.S. Air Force successfully tested an F-22 pilot commanding an autonomous drone, a key step in integrating AI into fighter squadrons.
details: An F-22 Raptor pilot has successfully directed an Anduril YFQ-44A Fury drone during a simulated combat exercise. The pilot issued tactical commands, which the drone interpreted and executed through flight maneuvers.

This test is part of the U.S. Air Force's Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program, aiming to integrate uncrewed aircraft into fighter squadrons. The goal is for drones to respond to pilot commands and operate autonomously, as pilots have a high workload.
The integration allows an F-22 pilot to assign tasks like monitoring for enemy air defenses to the drone, freeing the pilot to focus on primary missions such as engaging enemy fighters.

However, the CCA program still faces several hurdles before operational deployment. These include determining the drone's tactical autonomy limits, safe flight control, weapons authorization, and performance under electronic interference.
The Air Force must also integrate these drones into its logistics and supply chain, covering maintenance, service, weapons handling, and forward airbase operations.
Despite these challenges, the USAF views autonomous drones as a force multiplier, enabling a single pilot to command multiple aircraft for missions at a lower cost than using all-crewed planes.

An F-22 Raptor pilot has successfully directed an Anduril YFQ-44A Fury drone during a simulated combat exercise. The pilot issued tactical commands, which the drone interpreted and executed through flight maneuvers.

The integration allows an F-22 pilot to assign tasks like monitoring for enemy air defenses to the drone, freeing the pilot to focus on primary missions such as engaging enemy fighters.

However, the CCA program still faces several hurdles before operational deployment. These include determining the drone's tactical autonomy limits, safe flight control, weapons authorization, and performance under electronic interference.

The Air Force must also integrate these drones into its logistics and supply chain, covering maintenance, service, weapons handling, and forward airbase operations.

Despite these challenges, the USAF views autonomous drones as a force multiplier, enabling a single pilot to command multiple aircraft for missions at a lower cost than using all-crewed planes.
